title: Mapping trapped water in spent nuclear fuel assembly and its internal structures immediately after drainage
abstract: This study quantitatively evaluates the initial residual water remaining after drainage in a pressurized water reactor (PLUS7) fuel assembly, a critical boundary condition determining the efficiency and success of the vacuum drying process in spent nuclear fuel dry storage. To investigate the hydrodynamic trapping mechanisms, multi-mode drainage tests—including gravity drainage, 2 bar compressed air purge, 2 bar helium gas purge, and a hybrid helium purge with a water pump—were conducted on systematically modularized assembly components (top and bottom nozzles, spacer grids, and active fuel rod unit sections). Results demonstrated that simple gravity drainage would leave a massive 8,460.42 ± 20.30 g of water across a full-scale assembly, necessitating active pressurized drainage. The application of a compressed air purge reduced the total residual water to 3,957.00 ± 20.30 g, whereas helium gas purging further decreased it to 3,550.28 ± 20.30 g due to its superior diffusivity and micro-flow-channel penetrability. Notably, the hybrid method combining a downstream water pump and helium gas recorded the lowest total residual water of 3,495.08 ± 20.30 g. Although the pump's hydraulic resistance slightly degraded drainage efficiency in small single components, it significantly extended the flow residence time in the vast active fuel rod sections—which account for over 96% of the trapped water—thereby maximizing the duration of the helium gas's aerodynamic shear force to effectively remove the viscous liquid film. The established quantitative database provides a data-driven operational strategy to minimize residual water, supporting safety evaluations and process reliability for long-term dry storage licensing.

title: Gamma-Ray Shielding, Structural Characterization and Radiation Hazard Assessment of Natural, Compacted, and Calcined Gypsum
abstract: The effects of mechanical compaction and thermal treatment on the gamma-ray shielding performance of natural gypsum collected from South Sinai, Egypt were investigated. Radiological hazard indices were evaluated to assess the radiological safety of the investigated gypsum. Structural and chemical characterization was carried out using X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy (XRF), X-ray diffraction (XRD) and Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) analyses. Gamma-ray attenuation parameters, including the mass attenuation coefficient (MAC), linear attenuation coefficient (LAC), half-value layer (HVL), and mean free path (MFP), were determined experimentally over the energy range 59.53–1408.01 keV and compared with theoretical values obtained from XCOM and Phy-X/PSD. The results showed that mechanical compaction improved the shielding performance by increasing the bulk density, whereas calcination altered the attenuation behavior depending on the treatment temperature. Among all investigated samples, the gypsum compacted at 150 bar exhibited the highest shielding performance. At 662 keV, the LAC increased from 0.132 cm -1 at 50 bar to 0.1826 cm -1 at 150 bar, corresponding to an improvement of approximately 38%. These findings indicate that Egyptian gypsum is a cost-effective material with potential for gamma-ray shielding applications, particularly after mechanical compaction.

title: Non-Ambipolarity of Microturbulent Transport
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>When exact magnetic surfaces are assumed to exist, the gyrokinetic theory of microturbulence gives the same radial transport for ions and electrons.  But, exact magnetic surfaces do not exist in the presence of what is called electrostatic microturbulence.  When the plasma pressure is non-zero, a turbulent electric potential is accompanied by a  turbulent magnetic field, which splits the rational magnetic surfaces with which it resonates.  If the magnetic field is assumed to have an ideal topology-conserving evolution, delta function current densities arise on resonant surfaces.  The singularity of the current density allows islands to open quickly, but there is no singularity that allows a rapid closure.  Islands remain and do not flutter into and out of existence.  A relative rotation of the electron fluid in neighboring island chains produces a non-dissipative force that can lock the islands together  and produce a non-ambipolar transport.  At sufficient plasma pressure, the islands associated with different resonant rational surfaces can overlap.  When this occurs some magnetic field lines will cross the entire radial region occupied by overlapping islands.  The effect on the electron fluid is to create a viscosity-like force, which is dissipative and tends to remove gradients in the electron rotation.  This also produces a non-ambipolar transport.  Under many assumptions, the island locking force is larger than the viscosity-like force.</jats:p>

title: Assessing the effect of error field penetration during plasma current ramp-up in the DIII-D tokamak
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This work provides evidence that established error field penetration threshold scalings remain applicable during plasma current ramp-up. In dedicated DIII-D experiments with imposed n=1 perturbations during extended Ip ramps, an apparent empirical threshold is found between 2 and 3 kA of applied 3D coil current, above which MHD modes are seeded. The imposed perturbation couples to the rational surfaces present during the ramp, seeding near the q=4 surface and penetrating as an m/n=3/1 mode by the end of the perturbation phase. To interpret these observations, multi-machine penetration threshold scalings are combined with equilibrium-based overlap metrics from the GPEC code, including the in-situ error fields of the device. This modeling reproduces the observed onset in the amplitude scan and classifies mode seeding across a database of 12 ramp-up discharges spanning a range of plasma currents and densities. Across this database, the seeding seems to be controlled by the applied 3D coil current rather than by the plasma current or its ramp rate. Accounting for the in-situ error fields is found to be important for reliable prediction. These results are consistent with the robustness of scaling-based penetration metrics when coupled to detailed 3D field modeling under transient ramp-up conditions, and suggest the importance of accounting for in-situ error fields when assessing additional externally induced perturbations. This work is motivated by future tokamaks in which transient, non-axisymmetric error fields can arise during startup, for example from closed-loop, passive runaway electron mitigation coils energized by loop voltage ramping up plasma current.</jats:p>

title: Measurements, Risk Assessment, and Source Apportionment of Radioactivity Levels in Soil of Okaba and Okobo Coalfields and Environs, Ankpa, Kogi State, Nigeria
abstract: Coal mining can elevate natural radioactivity in surrounding environments, posing radiological risks. This study assessed the activity concentrations of 238U, 232Th, and 40K in 40 composite soil samples collected from active and abandoned mines, waste dumps, farmlands, and residential areas in the Okaba and Okobo coalfields, Kogi State, Nigeria, using high-purity germanium gamma spectrometry. Radiological hazards were evaluated (radium equivalent activity, absorbed dose rates, annual effective doses, hazard indices, annual gonadal equivalent dose, excess lifetime cancer risk), and source apportionment was performed using radionuclide ratios, Pearson correlation, and principal component analysis (PCA).Mean activities (238U: 77.1 Bq·kg−1; 232Th: 81.9 Bq·kg−1; and 40K: 1193 Bq·kg−1) were significantly higher than global averages (p < .001). Ten locations (25%) exceeded the 370 Bq·kg−1 radium equivalent safety limit. The mean absorbed dose rate (570 nGy·h−1) was approximately 10× the global average, and the excess lifetime cancer risk (6.36 × 10−3) exceeded the global reference value (0.29 × 10−3, United Nations Scientific Committee on The Effects of Atomic Radiation report from 2000) by a factor of 20.Source apportionment using PCA with Kaiser criterion (eigenvalues > 1) revealed two dominant sources: geological (66.4% of variance, 232Th and 40K) and anthropogenic mining (31.1%, 238U). The elevated radiological parameters indicate potential long-term health risks, with uranium enrichment linked to artisanal mining activities. Urgent regulatory enforcement is required, aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals 3 (health), 12 (responsible consumption), and 15 (life on land).

title: Development of a Technical, Economic, Risk, and Adoption Assessment Framework for the Evaluation of Modernization Opportunities
abstract: The efficient and cost-effective operation of nuclear power plants is essential for ensuring their long-term economic sustainability and competitiveness. Although the nuclear industry has achieved record high reliability and capacity factors, multiple cost savings and modernization opportunities exist as technology continues to progress. Identifying and objectively screening these opportunities is a periodic and essential plant activity for reducing overall costs and maintaining a modern fleet with up-to-date technology.However, evaluating these opportunities can be challenging for nuclear plant experts and engineers due to the complexity of the plant processes and the constant evolution of new technologies. These challenges often result in the use of costly consultants or potentially the miscalculation of risks or benefits of new technology.To address these challenges, this paper presents the technical, economic, and risk assessment (TERA) framework for screening and evaluating modernization opportunities. This novel framework combines several methodologies, such as process mapping and probabilistic modeling, to help nuclear plants perform quantitative assessments that can aid plant personnel in making risk-informed decisions for technology investments. This novel combination of methodologies creates a systematic evaluation that can reduce investment risk and ensure confidence in the integration of new technologies into existing processes. This paper introduces the TERA framework and presents a case study with initial quantitative results.

title: Deep learning models for ADITYA-U MHD equilibrium
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This work presents an integrated deep learning framework for rapid magnetohydrodynamic equilibrium estimation in the ADITYA-U tokamak. A free-boundary equilibrium database containing 100,760 cases was generated using the pyIPREQ Grad-Shafranov solver from experimentally derived operating conditions spanning 766 ADITYA-U plasma discharges, with constraints representative of circular limiter plasmas near the flat-top phase. The database was used to develop a cascaded framework for predicting scalar equilibrium quantities, 1d safety factor profiles, and 2d poloidal flux profiles. Dense neural networks, principal component analysis, convolutional neural networks and physics-informed neural networks were investigated within this framework. The error propagation, cross-models consistency and ablation study of Grad-Shafranov residual were performed for the proposed framework. Across the test dataset, the models achieve median mean absolute errors of 1e-2 for the safety factor profile and 2e-3 for the normalized poloidal flux profile. The largest model requires approximately 1 ms per equilibrium inference on a multi-core CPU. The results demonstrate the potential of the framework as a fast surrogate for equilibrium analysis, experiment planning and real-time plasma control applications for ADITYA-U experiments.</jats:p>

title: Transient coupling analysis for helical cruciform fuel core based on 3D method of characteristics and refined subchannel method
abstract: Helical cruciform fuel (HCF) offers enhanced heat transfer, stronger coolant mixing, and improved safety potential for advanced water-cooled reactors, but its complex geometry makes high-fidelity neutronics/thermal-hydraulic (N/TH) coupling analysis challenging. In this study, a coupled framework for HCF cores is developed by integrating the 3D Method of Characteristics code OpenMOC with the refined subchannel code RESTAR-HF. Quarter-core assembly-feedback calculations are first compared with OpenMC/RESTAR-HF results. On this basis, full-core pin-by-pin feedback coupling is performed, and the method is further extended to transient analysis of a rod ejection accident starting from hot full power. For this HFP case, results show that the peak core power reaches 108.451% at 0.04 s, while fuel centerline temperature, clad surface temperature, and minimum departure from nucleate boiling ratio satisfy the predefined criteria for the analyzed transient.
